segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Academic Monologue and Phase Assessment: Listening Practice

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You will hear a conversation between two students, Li Wei and Sarah, discussing an academic monologue and their phase assessment.

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Hi Sarah, have you listened to the academic monologue for our listening assessment yet?

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Not yet. I heard it's about urban gardening. Is that right?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Yes, it's a talk by a researcher named Dr. Chen. She discusses how city farms can improve food security. But I found some parts difficult because of the complex noun phrases.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Like what?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Well, she says things like 'the increasing reliance on imported produce in densely populated urban areas'. That's a long noun phrase with modifiers.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: I see. So the main clause is something like 'reliance is increasing'?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Exactly. The subject is 'reliance', and 'on imported produce' modifies it. The passive voice is also used a lot, for example, 'food security is being threatened by climate change'.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: That's a passive construction. The focus is on the action, not the doer.

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Right. And there are also reduced relative clauses, like 'crops grown on rooftops' instead of 'crops that are grown on rooftops'.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: That's tricky. I need to practise identifying the main clause. So, for the assessment, do we have to answer questions about the monologue?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Yes, there are ten questions. Some are multiple choice, some are fill-in-the-blank, and there's a true/false/not given section.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: True/false/not given? I find those hard because sometimes the information isn't there.

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Me too. But the teacher said for 'not given', we need to check if the fact is missing. For example, if the question asks about the cost of urban gardens, but the monologue doesn't mention cost, then it's not given.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: That makes sense. What about the fill-in-the-blank? How many words can we use?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Usually no more than two words. And the answers must be exactly as they appear in the recording.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: OK. So, when is the assessment?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: It's next Friday, the 15th. We have to submit our answers online by 5 pm.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: And where do we submit?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: On the course website, under 'Assessments'. There's a link called 'Phase Assessment 1'.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Thanks. I should start listening to the monologue again. Do you have any tips for understanding the grammar?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: I find it helpful to underline the main verb and subject first, then look at the modifiers. Also, for passive sentences, ask 'who or what is doing the action?' even if it's not stated.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Good idea. I'll try that. Oh, one more thing: is the monologue available for download?

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: Yes, it's on the course website as an MP3 file. You can listen as many times as you want before the assessment.

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Great. I'll download it now. Thanks for your help, Li Wei.

segments.speaker: Li Wei
segments.text: No problem. Good luck!

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Library Orientation: Using the Academic Resource Centre

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Academic Resource Centre. My name is Sarah, and I’m the head librarian here. I’ll be giving you a short orientation to help you make the most of our facilities. Please feel free to take notes, and I’ll be happy to answer questions at the end.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, let me explain the layout. The ground floor, where we are now, houses the main service desk, the new books display, and the café. This is also where you can collect reserved items and ask staff for general help. The first floor is dedicated to silent study. You’ll find individual desks and power sockets there, but please note that conversations are not allowed. The second floor contains group study rooms, which can be booked online up to two weeks in advance. Each room is equipped with a whiteboard and a large screen, so they are ideal for collaborative projects and presentations.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, about borrowing. Undergraduate students can borrow up to ten items at a time, while postgraduate students may borrow up to fifteen. The standard loan period is three weeks, but you can renew items online twice, provided no one else has reserved them. If you return an item late, a fine of 50 pence per day will be charged. However, if you have a disability or a long-term health condition, you may be exempt from fines—please speak to the service desk for details.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: We also offer a range of digital resources. Our online catalogue gives you access to thousands of e-books and academic journals. You can log in using your student ID and password. If you need help with research, you can book a one-to-one session with a subject librarian. These sessions last 30 minutes and are available Monday to Friday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, a few practical points. The library is open 24 hours a day during term time, but during vacations we close at 8 p.m. on weekdays and at 6 p.m. at weekends. There is a small kitchen on the ground floor with a microwave and a fridge, but hot food is not allowed in the study areas. Also, please remember to bring your student card—you’ll need it to enter the building after 10 p.m. and to borrow books.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: That’s all from me. Are there any questions?

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Simulated Academic Listening: Research Project Discussion

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for coming. Today we need to finalise the plan for your research project on urban green spaces. Let's start with the timeline. Maria, could you remind us of the submission dates?

segments.speaker: MARIA
segments.text: Yes, of course. The proposal is due on the 15th of March, and the final report must be submitted by the 30th of April. Oh, wait, I think I said that wrong—the final report is due on the 30th of April, not the 3rd of May. Sorry about that.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Thank you, Maria. So, proposal 15th March, final report 30th April. Now, let's discuss the research methods. David, you were going to look at questionnaires.

segments.speaker: DAVID
segments.text: That's right. I've designed a questionnaire with 20 questions. It will be distributed to 100 residents in three different neighbourhoods. The questions cover frequency of visits, activities, and satisfaction levels.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. And what about interviews?

segments.speaker: DAVID
segments.text: We also plan to conduct 15 semi-structured interviews with park users. Each interview should last about 30 minutes.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: That sounds reasonable. Now, about the literature review. Who is handling that?

segments.speaker: MARIA
segments.text: I am. I've already found 12 relevant articles, but I need to narrow them down to about 8 for the final review. I'll focus on studies from the last five years.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Excellent. Remember to include both quantitative and qualitative studies. Now, let's talk about data analysis. David, will you use software?

segments.speaker: DAVID
segments.text: Yes, we'll use SPSS for the questionnaire data and NVivo for the interviews. I've used SPSS before, but I'm less familiar with NVivo, so I might need some training.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: The university offers workshops on NVivo. I'll send you the schedule. Now, Maria, you mentioned something about ethical approval?

segments.speaker: MARIA
segments.text: Yes, we need to submit an ethics form before we start collecting data. The form requires details about informed consent and data storage. We should submit it by the end of February.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Correct. And have you thought about how you'll present your findings?

segments.speaker: DAVID
segments.text: We plan to write a report and also give a presentation to the department. The presentation will be in the last week of May.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. Finally, let's discuss the budget. Do you need any funding?

segments.speaker: MARIA
segments.text: We need about £200 for printing questionnaires and £150 for transcription services. So a total of £350.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: I'll see what I can do. Okay, I think we've covered everything. Let's meet again next week to review the questionnaire design.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: The Silent Library: A Lecture on Acoustic Design in Academic Spaces

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something we often take for granted in academic buildings: acoustic design. Specifically, I'll discuss how the design of libraries and study spaces affects concentration, and why some seemingly quiet rooms are actually worse for learning than noisy ones. This lecture is based on a simulated case study of a university library renovation, so please treat the details as illustrative rather than as research findings.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Let's start with a common misconception. Many people assume that the quietest possible environment is always best for studying. However, research in environmental psychology suggests that complete silence can be distracting for some learners. In one simulated experiment, students in an anechoic chamber—a room with almost no echo—reported feeling uncomfortable and found it harder to focus than students in a room with mild background noise. The reason is that in absolute silence, small sounds like a pen clicking or a chair squeaking become highly noticeable. So, the first key point is that a moderate level of ambient sound, around 40 to 50 decibels, may actually support concentration for many people.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, let's move on to the design features that can create this balanced acoustic environment. One important element is the use of sound-absorbing materials. For example, installing acoustic panels on walls and ceilings can reduce reverberation—the persistence of sound after the source has stopped. Reverberation time is measured in seconds, and in a typical classroom, it should be around 0.6 seconds for good speech intelligibility. In a large lecture hall, however, a longer reverberation time of up to 1.2 seconds may be acceptable because the space is bigger and sound needs to travel further.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Another feature is the layout of furniture. Open-plan study areas with long tables and hard surfaces tend to amplify noise because sound waves bounce off these surfaces. In contrast, arranging study carrels with high partitions and soft seating can help contain sound. Interestingly, the simulated renovation project found that simply adding carpet and curtains reduced perceived noise levels by about 30 percent, even though the actual sound level remained the same. This shows that psychological factors—how people perceive sound—are just as important as physical measurements.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, I want to mention the role of background music or white noise. Some libraries now provide white-noise machines or allow students to use noise-cancelling headphones. While these can be helpful, they are not a substitute for good acoustic design. In fact, relying too much on headphones may lead to increased listening fatigue. The best approach is to combine thoughtful architectural design with personal strategies.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: To sum up, effective acoustic design in academic spaces is not about eliminating all sound but about managing it. Moderate ambient noise, sound-absorbing materials, smart furniture layout, and personal tools like headphones all play a part. Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take questions after the break.
